name: Cysteamine
lead: Cysteamine (2-aminoethanethiol, mercaptamine) is a small organosulfur compound containing both an amine and a thiol group. Mammals make it naturally during the breakdown of coenzyme A, and it is used as a medicine for nephropathic cystinosis, a lysosomal storage disease in which cystine accumulates in cells.[1]

In appearance care, a topical cysteamine preparation is used to lighten skin darkened by melasma, post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation or sun exposure, and is described as a non-hydroquinone option for people who want to even out skin tone.[1][2][3] A 2025 double-blind randomized trial compared an overnight leave-on cream containing 5 percent cysteamine and ectoine with 4 percent hydroquinone cream in melasma.[4] A 2022 review of topical melasma treatments describes cysteamine, with tranexamic acid, as an agent of recent interest because of good tolerability, while noting that more trials are warranted.[2]

For appearance, the goal is a more even complexion: cysteamine is applied to patches of melasma, to the dark marks left after acne or irritation, and to sun-related spots, usually as a leave-on or short-contact cream alongside daily sunscreen.[22][21] A 2025 systematic review of eight trial studies reported that cysteamine lowered Melasma Area and Severity Index scores by 1.5 to 10.07 points (mean 5.73), with mild reactions such as redness, itching, dryness, tingling and burning.[21]

Dermatology reviews list cysteamine hydrochloride among oral and topical agents used for hyperpigmentation, while noting that pigmentation treatments often take long to work and carry adverse effects.[3] A practical limit noted in a general reference is instability of the molecule, which oxidizes in air to cystamine.[5]

paras: Cysteamine occupies two separate worlds. In medicine it is an old, prescription-only drug for a rare inherited disease, cystinosis, where it clears cystine from cells.[1] In skincare it is a newer entrant, promoted as a depigmenting ingredient for melasma and other dark patches that is not hydroquinone.[22][2] Formulations, concentrations and goals differ between the two, and most pharmacology and safety data in this article come from the oral and eye-drop medical products rather than skin creams.

Melasma is a common pigment disorder in which brown patches appear on sun-exposed skin, particularly the face. Its cause is not fully understood; sunlight, hormones such as pregnancy or oral contraceptives, genetics and skin type are all described as contributors, and it tends to relapse.[22] Topical agents lighten the patches gradually, so the appearance goal is a slow fade rather than a quick change.

Topical cysteamine is used for melasma, post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation (dark marks left after acne or irritation) and sun-related dark spots, with the aim of a more even complexion.[1][2] Reviews of topical melasma treatment and hyperpigmentation management list it among agents beyond hydroquinone and triple combination cream, which remain the best-studied options.[2][3] The 2021 pigment-disorder review places cysteamine hydrochloride in the group of therapies given by mouth or topically after first-line agents such as hydroquinone, kojic acid and glycolic acid, with chemical peels and lasers as second-line approaches.[3]

Wikipedia lists topical use for skin darkened by post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation, sun exposure or melasma as one of its uses besides cystinosis, and describes it as available only by prescription as a drug.[1]

Cysteamine is indicated for cystinosis under the brand names Cystagon and Procysbi and as eye drops; the US label for the ophthalmic product (Cystadrops) lists treatment of corneal cystine crystal deposits in adults and children with cystinosis.[1][6] The first report of benefit in cystinosis dates to the 1950s, and a 1987 trial in children established therapy for nephropathic cystinosis.[1][7] It has also been studied for Huntington's disease, mitochondrial disease, cystic fibrosis, fatty liver disease and depression, and in the past as an antidote for paracetamol overdose.[8][9][10][11][12][13]

For hyperpigmentation, the main controlled evidence is the 2025 multicenter double-blind randomized comparison of 5 percent cysteamine with ectoine against 4 percent hydroquinone in melasma.[4] A 2022 systematic review of 80 papers on topical melasma treatments reports that triple combination therapy and hydroquinone remain the most well-studied agents, that ascorbic acid, azelaic acid, glycolic acid, kojic acid, salicylic acid and niacinamide have evidence as adjuvant therapies, and that cysteamine and tranexamic acid have become agents of interest for their tolerability, with more studies called for.[2] Published trials of topical cysteamine are modest in size relative to hydroquinone.
In cystinosis, a 1987 trial in children established benefit of cysteamine therapy for nephropathic disease, and enteric-coated bitartrate formulations have since been studied in patients.[7][15]

sections.h: Topical use for pigmentation in practice
paras: Wikipedia's melasma article describes 5% cysteamine hydrochloride as an over-the-counter option that appears to act by inhibiting the melanin synthesis pathway, alongside hydroquinone (2% over the counter, 4% by prescription in the US), tretinoin, azelaic acid and kojic acid; it notes that combination therapy such as hydroquinone, tretinoin and a steroid has tended to outperform simpler regimens.[22] It adds that effects are gradual, that strict sun protection is needed because ultraviolet and visible light can stimulate pigment, and that melasma often returns, especially in summer.[22]

Dermatology reviewers describe cysteamine and tranexamic acid as newer options with good tolerability that need more study; the 2022 review concluded that they can serve as adjunct or maintenance treatments while triple combination therapy remains the standard of care and hydroquinone the benchmark for other agents.[23] Cysteamine is also sold as an ingredient in cosmetic creams for dark spots, and the molecule's tendency to oxidise in air affects how products are formulated and packaged.[5]

The 2025 randomized trial compared an overnight leave-on cysteamine and ectoine cream with 4 percent hydroquinone in melasma.[4] Reviews summarise topical melasma and hyperpigmentation therapies.[2][3]

The 2025 randomized trial ran from January to March 2024 at three hospitals in Indonesia, comparing 5% cysteamine with ectoine against 4% hydroquinone with ectoine, and measured modified MASI scores and skin-analyser readings plus quality-of-life questionnaires (MELASQoL and DLQI). Both groups improved; the cysteamine group improved slightly more, but the difference was not statistically significant, and quality of life improved similarly in both. The authors concluded that either regimen is a viable option.[24][4] A separate 2025 systematic review of eight trial studies published between 2013 and 2023 reported MASI reductions of 1.5 to 10.07 and only mild adverse reactions.[21]

Outside pigmentation, clinical studies include a 1987 trial of cysteamine in children with nephropathic cystinosis,[7] pharmacokinetic work in cystinosis patients,[14] enteric-coated bitartrate studies,[15] a 2017 randomized placebo-controlled trial in 96 patients with early Huntington's disease,[8] registered trials in cystinosis, mitochondrial disease, cystic fibrosis, fatty liver in children and major depression,[9][10][11][12][13][16][17] and a 2026 gene therapy study in cystinosis in which oral cysteamine was withdrawn before infusion.[18]

Wikipedia reports that oral cysteamine labels warn of Ehlers-Danlos-like symptoms, severe skin rashes, gastrointestinal ulcers or bleeding, central nervous system effects including seizures and encephalopathy, low white blood cell counts and idiopathic intracranial hypertension, with bad breath, skin odor, nausea, vomiting and abdominal pain also reported.[1] The eye drop label lists eye pain, blurred vision, irritation, redness and ocular deposits as the most common effects and warns about benign intracranial hypertension reported with oral use.[6] The label notes teratogenicity in rats at oral doses 240 to 960 times the human ophthalmic dose and says adequate human data are lacking.[6]
For topical skin use, odor and instability are practical drawbacks; detailed adverse event rates have not been reported.

Wikipedia lists common oral effects as bad breath, skin odor, nausea, vomiting, stomach pain, diarrhea and loss of appetite; eye drop effects include light sensitivity, redness, eye pain, headache and visual field defects.[1]

In cystinosis, cysteamine enters lysosomes and converts cystine into cysteine and a cysteine-cysteamine mixed disulfide, both of which can leave the lysosome.[1][6] The mechanism in skin is described in dermatology reviews as involving tyrosinase and related inhibition and antioxidant activity.[3]

In cystinosis, patients lack a functioning cystinosin transporter, so cystine builds up in lysosomes, crystallizes and damages cells; cysteamine enters the lysosome and converts cystine into cysteine and a cysteine-cysteamine mixed disulfide that can exit. It also promotes cysteine transport into cells.[1] Mammals also produce cysteamine as the precursor of hypotaurine.[1]

Population pharmacokinetic work in cystinosis patients has modelled how cysteamine exposure relates to its effect on white-cell cystine levels.[14] Enteric-coated bitartrate formulations have been studied as a way to deliver it.[15] Wikipedia notes that extended-release capsules should not be taken with proton pump inhibitors or alcohol, which can release the drug too quickly, and that cysteamine does not inhibit cytochrome P450 enzymes.[1]

Cysteamine has the formula HSCH2CH2NH2, a molar mass of about 77 g/mol, and is a water-soluble white solid melting at roughly 95 to 97 degrees Celsius. It is often supplied as the hydrochloride or bitartrate salt.[1] It oxidizes in air to the disulfide cystamine, which complicates formulation of skin products.[1][5]

The therapeutic effect on cystinosis was reported in the 1950s; the US approved cysteamine for cystinosis in 1994 and an extended-release form in 2013.[1] A 1977 review noted that intravenous cysteamine appeared effective in preventing liver damage from acetaminophen overdose if given within about ten hours, and a history of paracetamol poisoning discusses early antidotes.[19][20]

Cysteamine is marketed for cystinosis as Cystagon (immediate-release capsules), Procysbi (extended-release capsules) and eye drops for corneal cystine crystals, all prescription products.[1][6] For skin, dermatology reviews discuss it as a hydroquinone alternative with good tolerability.[2][3] Practical limits mentioned in reference texts are the molecule's instability in air and, for oral use, odor effects.[1][5]

lore.intro: In skincare discussion cysteamine is raised as a hydroquinone alternative for melasma, post-acne marks and uneven tone, often by people who want a non-hydroquinone product.[2][3]

claims.claim: Topical cysteamine is a hydroquinone alternative for melasma and dark marks
claims.believers: Proponents describe it as a non-hydroquinone option for lightening darkened skin, with good tolerability.[1][2]
claims.experts: A 2022 review calls cysteamine an agent of recent interest because of tolerability but says more trials are warranted, while hydroquinone and triple combination therapy remain best studied; a 2025 randomized trial found 5% cysteamine with ectoine and 4% hydroquinone both improved melasma, with no significant difference between them.[2][24]

claims.claim: Cysteamine lightens melasma with mild side effects
claims.believers: Users and brands emphasise low irritation compared with stronger lighteners.[2]
claims.experts: A 2025 systematic review of eight trial studies reported MASI score reductions and only mild reactions such as redness, itching, dryness, tingling and burning.[21]

claims.claim: Cysteamine can serve as a maintenance step after other treatments
claims.believers: Some practitioners describe using it to hold results between courses of stronger therapy.[2]
claims.experts: The 2022 review said cysteamine and tranexamic acid can serve as adjunct or maintenance treatments, while noting that long-term studies are lacking.[23]

claims.claim: Sunscreen is part of any pigment routine
claims.believers: Dermatology sources and skincare communities describe daily sun protection alongside lighteners.[3]
claims.experts: Melasma is chronic and relapsing, and small amounts of sun can bring it back after it fades.[22]
